intro: In 1325 a young man left Morocco on a donkey and spent the next thirty years crossing a world that was already connected: by camel caravans over the Sahara, by monsoon ships across the Indian Ocean, by Mongol relay roads across Asia. Two centuries later a silver coin dug from a mountain in the Andes could buy Chinese silk in the Philippines. This unit follows how the connected world of 1200 became the global world of 1750, and what that change cost the people who lived through it.

It is a story with no single hero and no single center. Song China built the richest economy on Earth. Muslim scholars kept and extended the world's science. Mali's gold paid for Italian art. Then plague crossed the same routes as silk, and a century later Europeans sailed into oceans they did not understand, met peoples they did not know existed, and set off the largest disaster and the largest forced migration in human history. Meanwhile rulers from Istanbul to Edo built states more powerful than any before them, and thinkers began to ask where a ruler's power really came from.

By the end you will be able to explain how goods, ideas and diseases traveled before and after 1492; why small Spanish forces toppled great empires; how silver and sugar tied five continents together; what the transatlantic slave trade was and how people resisted it; and how the Ottomans, Mughals, Qing, Tokugawa, Bourbons and English Parliament each answered the same question: what does a state's power rest on?
bigQuestion: How did the world become connected between 1200 and 1750, and who paid the price for those connections?

It moved all trade to the sea

test.q: Why did trade in the Indian Ocean depend on the monsoon?
choices: The winds reversed on a predictable schedule, carrying ships out and back
The monsoon brought rain that filled the harbors
Ships could only sail during storms
test.why: Sailors timed their voyages to the summer and winter monsoons, which blew steadily in opposite directions.

test.q: What did West Africa trade across the Sahara, and for what?
test.why: West Africa had abundant gold and little salt; the desert had salt mines and needed gold, so caravans carried each toward the other.

test.q: Which was a long-term effect of the Black Death in western Europe?
choices: Wages rose and peasants gained bargaining power
test.why: With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher pay and more freedom, and lords could not stop them.

test.q: What was Gutenberg's real contribution to printing?
choices: He invented the idea of printing
He carved the first wood blocks
He combined metal movable type, oil-based ink and a press into one system
test.why: Printing and movable type existed in Asia centuries earlier; Gutenberg's system made mass printing practical for European alphabets.

test.q: Which region was the richest and most populous in 1450?
test.why: China had the largest economy, biggest ships and oldest printing industry, though it had just ended its ocean voyages.

test.q: Why did small Spanish forces defeat the Aztec and Inca empires?

Disease, Indigenous allies, civil war, and steel and horses combined against them
The Aztec and Inca surrendered without fighting

test.q: Which food crossed from the Americas to Afro-Eurasia in the Columbian Exchange?
test.why: Potatoes, corn, tomatoes and chili peppers are American crops; wheat, sugar and coffee came from Afro-Eurasia.

test.q: Where did most silver from Potosí eventually end up?
choices: In China, exchanged for silk and other goods
test.why: China's demand for silver drew a large share of American output across the Pacific through Manila and around through Europe.

choices: About twelve and a half million

It had no effect on either
test.why: Printing carried Luther's theses and Galileo's drawings across Europe in months and let scholars compare exact copies.

test.q: Which ruler abolished the tax on non-Muslims and hosted debates among faiths?
test.why: Akbar ended the jizya in 1564 and gathered Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Christians to debate at Fatehpur Sikri.

test.q: What did the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and Locke's writing of 1690 together establish?
choices: That kings rule by divine right
That the ruler is under the law and governs by the consent of the governed
That England would become a republic
test.why: Parliament's Bill of Rights limited the crown, and Locke argued that government exists to protect rights with the people's consent.

story.title: The Man Who Could Not Stop Traveling
story.kicker: In 1325 a twenty-one-year-old law student left Morocco to pray in Mecca. He did not come home for almost thirty years.
paragraphs: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, a port on the northern tip of Morocco, in 1304. His family were judges and scholars of Islamic law. In June of 1325 he set out alone on a donkey for the *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca that every Muslim who can afford it is expected to make once. Mecca was more than three thousand miles away. He later wrote that he wept when he left his parents, and that he had no companion to cheer him.

He never really came back to the life he left. After Mecca he kept going: to Iraq and Persia, down the coast of East Africa to the stone city of Kilwa, north into the lands of the Mongol Golden Horde, then across the mountains into India. The sultan of Delhi hired him as a judge and later sent him as an ambassador toward China. Along the way he was shipwrecked, robbed, nearly executed and married several times. He said he reached China; some historians doubt how far he actually got.

What made such a journey possible? Everywhere he went, Ibn Battuta found people who shared his religion, his language of learning, Arabic, and his law. A judge from Morocco could find work in Delhi because Delhi's rulers used the same legal books he had studied at home. Muslim merchants ran hostels and mosques from Mali to Malaysia. He traveled through a connected world, not a series of walled-off kingdoms.

He also traveled in the shadow of the Mongols. Their empire had shattered old borders across Asia a century before, and the roads they guarded still carried silk, paper, gunpowder recipes and travelers like him. In 1348, on his way home, he met something else moving along those same roads: the plague. In Damascus he watched two thousand people die a day. He reached Morocco in 1349, then set off once more, this time south across the Sahara to the gold empire of Mali.

When he finally settled down, the sultan of Morocco ordered a young scholar to write down everything he remembered. The book, called simply the Travels, is one of the richest windows we have on the world of the 1300s. This chapter follows the routes he followed, from the Chinese ports that made the world's finest porcelain to the desert caravans that carried Africa's gold, and asks how the pieces fit together.
story.think: Ibn Battuta could work as a judge thousands of miles from home. What would a person today need in order to do the same thing?

lessons.title: Song China's Economic Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: Between about 960 and 1279, China under the Song dynasty built the most productive economy on Earth, driven by rice, iron, paper money and cities.
reading: Picture the city of Kaifeng around the year 1100. Shops stayed open at night. Restaurants served noodles and roast duck. Boats crowded the canals bringing rice from the south. Kaifeng may have held close to a million people, more than any city in Europe would hold for centuries. It was the capital of the *Song dynasty*, which ruled China from 960 to 1279. Historians call what happened under the Song an economic revolution, and the word is not an exaggeration.

The revolution started in the fields. Farmers adopted a fast-ripening rice from Champa, in what is now Vietnam, that let them harvest two crops a year. More food meant more people. China's population roughly doubled to about one hundred million by the early 1100s. Fewer hands were needed on farms, so more people could work in towns as weavers, potters, ironworkers and shopkeepers. Song iron foundries used coal and water-powered bellows and turned out iron on a scale Europe would not match for six hundred years.

Trade this large needed money that was easy to carry. Copper coins were heavy, so merchants in Sichuan began using paper receipts, and in the 1020s the Song government printed the world's first state *paper money*. The government also expanded the *civil service examination*, a test on classic texts that chose officials by merit rather than birth. Passing it took years of study, but the exam made learning valuable and helped create a huge market for printed books.

How do we know all this? Song officials kept detailed tax and production records, and painters recorded daily life. One long scroll from the early 1100s, attributed to the artist Zhang Zeduan, shows Kaifeng's streets crowded with camels, carts, teahouses and a great bridge packed with people. Look at that painting and you see an economy in motion: it is evidence you can read with your eyes.

words.d: the family that ruled China from 960 to 1279, a time of rapid economic growth and invention
printed notes that stand for value; first issued by a government in Song China in the 1020s
a test on classic texts that chose Chinese government officials by merit

look.cite: Standard dates from Song records and Shen Kuo's writings

check.q: What was the first step in the Song economic revolution?
choices: Fast-ripening rice let farmers grow more food
The government ended the civil service exam
Iron foundries switched from coal to wood
check.why: More food came first. Champa rice allowed two harvests a year, which let the population grow and freed people to work in towns.

Paper was rarer and more valuable than copper
The emperor banned all metal coins
Foreign traders refused to accept coins

lessons.title: Dar al-Islam and Its Scholars
lessons.mainIdea: By 1200 the Muslim world stretched from Spain to India, tied together by one faith, one language of learning and a shared body of knowledge.
reading: Muslims called the lands where Islam was practiced *Dar al-Islam*, the House of Islam. By 1200 it reached from Spain and Morocco across North Africa and the Middle East to Persia, Central Asia and northern India. It was never one empire for long. Yet a scholar in Cordoba and a scholar in Samarkand read the same Quran in the same Arabic, studied the same law and could argue about the same books. That shared culture is what let Ibn Battuta find work everywhere.

The knowledge those scholars shared was vast. In Baghdad in the 800s, the caliphs paid translators to turn Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Building on them, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations whose title gave us the word *algebra*. Ibn al-Haytham, around 1020, showed by experiment that we see because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, finished around 1025, was used to train doctors in Europe for five hundred years.

Two Chinese gifts helped. Paper reached the Islamic world in the 700s, and paper mills soon ran in Samarkand, Baghdad and Cairo. Cheap paper meant more books, and books needed libraries and schools. A *madrasa* was a college attached to a mosque where students learned law, grammar, logic and often mathematics and astronomy. Al-Azhar in Cairo, founded in the 970s, still operates today.

Historians read this era through the books that survive, but also through what does not. In 1258 a Mongol army captured Baghdad, killed the caliph and destroyed its libraries. Later writers said the river ran black with ink. That is probably a legend, but the loss was real. Learning did not die; it shifted to Cairo, Damascus, Persia and India. A civilization this widespread could absorb even a blow like Baghdad.

words.d: the House of Islam: all the lands where Muslims lived under Islamic law, from Spain to India
the branch of math that solves for unknown numbers; the word comes from al-Khwarizmi's Arabic book title
a college, usually attached to a mosque, where students studied law, religion and often science

look.title: Why Write a Math Book?
look.text: Al-Khwarizmi explained that he wrote his book on calculation to cover the things people actually need: dividing inheritances, settling lawsuits, trading, measuring land and digging canals. He said he chose the easiest and most useful parts of arithmetic for these tasks.
look.cite: Al-Khwarizmi, introduction to his book on algebra, Baghdad, about 820 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Al-Khwarizmi says math is for inheritance, trade and canals. What does that tell you about who paid for scholarship and why?

check.q: What held Dar al-Islam together when it was not one empire?
choices: A single army stationed in every city
One ruler chosen by all Muslims
A shared faith, language of learning and body of law
A ban on trade with non-Muslims
check.why: Political unity came and went. What lasted was a common religion, Arabic scholarship and legal tradition.

check.q: What did Ibn al-Haytham prove about sight?
choices: The eye sends out rays that touch objects
Light enters the eye from objects
check.why: By experiment he showed that light travels from objects into the eye, overturning an older Greek idea.

check.q: Which Chinese invention helped Islamic scholarship grow?
check.why: Paper made books cheap enough to fill libraries and madrasas. Mills in Samarkand and Baghdad produced it from the 700s.

lessons.title: The Mongol Peace
lessons.mainIdea: The Mongols conquered by terror, but the empire they built made travel across Asia safer and faster than ever before.
reading: In 1206 a Mongol chief named Temujin united the herding tribes of the steppe and took the title Genghis Khan. By his death in 1227 his horsemen had smashed kingdoms from northern China to Persia. His sons and grandsons pushed on into Russia, Iraq and southern China. The result was the largest connected land empire in history. Its armies were fast, disciplined and merciless: cities that resisted were often destroyed to frighten the next city into surrender.

Once the fighting stopped, something surprising happened. The Mongols were few, and they needed taxes, so they protected trade. They built the *yam*, a chain of relay stations with fresh horses spaced a day's ride apart, so messengers and merchants could cross Asia in weeks instead of months. Travelers carried a *paiza*, a metal tablet ordering local officials to give them food, shelter and horses. Historians call this period, roughly 1250 to 1350, the Pax Mongolica, the Mongol Peace.

Along those roads moved Chinese silk and porcelain, Persian carpets, gunpowder recipes, paper money, astronomers, doctors and missionaries. The Venetian merchant Marco Polo traveled to the court of Kublai Khan around 1275 and stayed for years. Mongol rulers usually let Buddhists, Muslims, Christians and Daoists worship freely, partly because they wanted useful people of every faith at court. After 1260 the empire split into four khanates, but trade among them continued.

The peace had a dark side. The same roads that carried silk carried disease. Fleas on rats in caravans and ships could move farther and faster than ever before. When plague broke out in Central Asia in the 1330s and 1340s, the Mongol network helped carry it west to the Black Sea and on to Europe and the Middle East. The connections the Mongols built made the world richer and, for a few terrible years, deadlier.

words.d: the Mongol system of relay stations with fresh horses that sped messengers and merchants across Asia
a metal tablet that ordered officials to give the bearer food, shelter and horses
the Mongol Peace, roughly 1250 to 1350, when Mongol rule made travel across Asia safer
one of the four Mongol states that the empire split into after 1260

look.title: A Merchant Describes the Relay Roads
look.text: Marco Polo wrote that on every main road out of the Khan's capital there was a post station every twenty-five or thirty miles, each with a fine building where messengers could sleep and hundreds of horses ready to ride. He said a messenger could cover in one day what normally took ten.
look.cite: Marco Polo, describing Kublai Khan's realm, dictated about 1298 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Polo's numbers may be exaggerated. What could a historian check against other evidence to decide how much to trust him?

check.q: Why did the Mongols protect merchants after their conquests?
choices: They needed the taxes that trade produced
Genghis Khan had been a merchant
Merchants had defeated them in battle
check.why: The Mongols were few and ruled many. Taxes on trade paid for their armies and courts, so they guarded the roads.

check.q: What was a paiza?
choices: A metal tablet ordering officials to help its bearer
check.why: The paiza was a passport of sorts. Officials who saw it had to give the traveler shelter, food and horses.

check.q: What would most likely have happened to the plague's spread if the Mongol roads had not existed?
choices: It would have spread more slowly and less widely
It would have started in Europe
It would have affected only Mongols
check.why: The plague moved with caravans and ships along the Mongol network. Without those connections, it would have traveled slower.

lessons.title: The Indian Ocean and the Monsoon
lessons.mainIdea: Predictable monsoon winds turned the Indian Ocean into a highway linking East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China.
reading: A sailor in Aden, at the mouth of the Red Sea, did not need a calendar to know when to leave for India. He needed the wind. Each summer the *monsoon* blows steadily from the southwest, pushing ships east toward India. Each winter it reverses and blows from the northeast, carrying them home. The winds were so regular that captains could plan round trips a year ahead. That reliability made the Indian Ocean the busiest sea in the world before 1500.

The ships were built for those winds. Arab and Indian shipwrights sewed the planks of their *dhows* together with coconut-fiber rope and rigged them with triangular lateen sails that could catch wind from the side. Chinese junks were larger, with watertight compartments and several masts. Ports grew where the winds and coasts met: Kilwa and Mogadishu on the East African coast, Aden and Hormuz in Arabia and Persia, Calicut in India, Malacca in Southeast Asia, and Quanzhou and Guangzhou in China.

Each region sold what others lacked. East Africa sent gold from the interior, ivory and enslaved people. India sent cotton cloth and pepper. The Spice Islands of Indonesia sent cloves and nutmeg. China sent silk and porcelain. Along the East African coast, trade created the *Swahili* culture: city-states whose people spoke a Bantu language filled with Arabic words, built houses of coral stone and practiced Islam. Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa in 1331 and called it one of the most beautifully built towns he had seen.

Archaeology backs up his account. Diggers at Kilwa and at Great Zimbabwe, far inland, have found fragments of Chinese porcelain and glass beads from India and Persia. Chinese coins turn up on Kenyan beaches. In 1405 the Chinese emperor sent Admiral Zheng He with a fleet of hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men on the first of seven voyages that reached India, Arabia and East Africa. Those voyages ended in 1433, but they showed how far the ocean's roads already ran.

words.d: a seasonal wind over the Indian Ocean that blows from the southwest in summer and the northeast in winter
an Arab or Indian sailing ship with sewn planks and a triangular lateen sail
the culture and language of the East African coast, blending Bantu, Arabic and Islamic elements

look.title: A Bowl at Great Zimbabwe
look.text: Imagine an archaeologist brushing dirt from a shard of blue-and-white porcelain inside the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe, hundreds of miles from the sea. The bowl was fired in a Chinese kiln. To get here it crossed the Indian Ocean in a junk or a dhow, landed at Kilwa, and was carried inland by traders, probably in exchange for gold that had been dug nearby.
look.prompt: What does one broken bowl prove, and what does it not prove, about the connection between Zimbabwe and China?

check.q: Why could Indian Ocean captains plan round trips a year in advance?
choices: The monsoon winds reversed direction on a regular schedule
check.why: The southwest monsoon carried ships east in summer and the northeast monsoon brought them back in winter, year after year.

check.q: What evidence besides Ibn Battuta's writing shows that Kilwa traded with Asia?
choices: Chinese porcelain and Indian beads found by archaeologists
check.why: Objects dug up at Kilwa and Great Zimbabwe came from China, India and Persia, confirming the long-distance trade.

check.q: Swahili culture is best described as
choices: a Chinese colony on the African coast
a blend of African, Arabic and Islamic elements created by trade
check.why: Swahili speakers used a Bantu language with Arabic words, built coral-stone towns and practiced Islam, all shaped by ocean trade.

lessons.title: Gold, Salt and the Empire of Mali
lessons.mainIdea: Camel caravans across the Sahara traded West African gold for salt and made Mali one of the richest states of its age.
reading: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth, and for centuries people crossed it the way sailors crossed the sea. The ship was the camel. A camel can carry heavy loads and go days without water, and a *caravan* of hundreds of camels could cover the roughly two-month journey from Morocco to the Niger River. Caravans traveled from oasis to oasis, guided by people who knew the wells, the stars and the shifting dunes.

The trade rested on a simple exchange. West Africa had gold in its rivers and mines but almost no salt, which people need to live and to preserve food. The desert had salt: at Taghaza, workers cut slabs of it from the ground, and houses there were built of salt blocks. Caravans carried salt south and gold north. That gold ended up in coins from Cairo to Venice. Before 1500 most of the gold in the Mediterranean world came from West Africa.

The state that controlled the gold's route grew powerful. Around 1235 a leader named Sundiata founded the empire of *Mali* on the upper Niger. Its most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made the hajj to Mecca in 1324. He traveled with thousands of followers and so much gold that prices in Cairo were still low years later from all the gold he gave away. A map made in Spain in 1375 shows him seated on a throne holding a golden nugget. His fame had crossed the desert and the sea.

Mali's wealth also bought learning. The city of *Timbuktu*, on the desert's edge, became a center of Islamic scholarship, with mosques, teachers and a busy trade in handwritten books. Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352 and praised how safe the roads were and how strictly people kept their prayers. He also complained about customs he found strange. His mixed report is a reminder that a traveler's view is one point of view, not the whole truth.

words.d: a group of merchants and pack animals, usually camels, traveling together across the desert
a West African empire founded around 1235 that controlled the gold trade on the upper Niger
a trading city on the edge of the Sahara that became a center of Islamic learning under Mali

look.title: The Gold That Flooded Cairo
look.text: An Egyptian official recorded that when Mansa Musa passed through Cairo, he and his followers spent and gave away so much gold that its value in the city dropped and had still not fully recovered twelve years later.
look.cite: Al-Umari, Egyptian scholar and official, writing in the 1330s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why would giving away gold make gold worth less? What does this story suggest about how much gold Mali controlled?

check.q: What did the desert supply that West Africa lacked?
check.why: Salt from mines like Taghaza was scarce in the gold-rich south. Caravans carried salt south and gold north.

check.q: How do we know Mansa Musa's fame reached Europe?
choices: A Spanish map from 1375 shows him holding a gold nugget
He wrote letters to the pope
check.why: The Catalan Atlas of 1375 pictured the ruler of Mali with gold, showing that Europeans knew of his wealth.

check.q: Why should a historian be careful using Ibn Battuta's account of Mali?
choices: He was paid by Mali's enemies
He judged what he saw by his own customs and gave one point of view
check.why: He praised Mali's safety and piety but complained about customs he found odd. His view is valuable but is only one outsider's view.

lessons.title: Travelers as Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Accounts by travelers like Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta are rich sources, but historians test them against other evidence before trusting them.
reading: Much of what we know about the world of 1300 comes from a handful of travelers who wrote things down. Marco Polo, a merchant from Venice, left for Asia in 1271 and returned in 1295. He dictated his story in a Genoese prison to a writer of romances. Ibn Battuta dictated his to a scholar in Morocco about 1355. Both books were bestsellers in their day. Both are also full of problems. Neither man kept a diary, so they recalled events years later.

So historians *corroborate*: they check one source against others. Polo described paper money, coal burned as fuel and the yam relay stations. Chinese records confirm all three. That raises our trust in him. But he never mentions the Great Wall, tea or the binding of women's feet, which makes some scholars wonder how much of China he saw. Ibn Battuta's description of Kilwa matches the ruins archaeologists have excavated. Parts of his account of China, however, may be borrowed from other writers.

Travelers also carried *bias*, a slant that shapes what a person notices and how they judge it. Polo measured everything by Venice and marveled at wealth. Ibn Battuta measured everything by Islamic law and was quick to praise piety or condemn its absence. Neither wrote much about the poor, about women's daily lives or about the enslaved people who rowed ships and carried loads. What a source leaves out is evidence too.

The best way to read these books is with a map, a timeline and a second source open beside them. When Polo and Ibn Battuta and a Chinese official all describe the same port, their agreements are probably true and their differences are worth arguing about. That habit of cross-checking is what turns a good story into history.

words.d: to confirm a source by checking it against other, independent sources
a slant in a source that shapes what its author noticed, praised, ignored or condemned
an account or object made by someone who lived through the events being studied

look.title: Money Made From Bark
look.text: Marco Polo reported that the Great Khan's mint in his capital made money from the inner bark of mulberry trees, cut into pieces of different sizes, stamped with the Khan's seal, and that everyone in his lands was required to accept it as payment on pain of death.
look.cite: Marco Polo, on the paper money of Kublai Khan, dictated about 1298 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Chinese records confirm that the Mongols issued paper money. How does that agreement change how you read the rest of Polo's book?

check.q: What does it mean to corroborate a source?
choices: To translate it into a new language
To check it against independent evidence
To copy it word for word
check.why: Historians confirm a claim by finding other sources, such as records or archaeology, that support it.

check.q: Why do some scholars doubt parts of Marco Polo's account?
choices: He never mentions things like the Great Wall or tea
Chinese records say paper money did not exist
He claimed to have invented the compass
check.why: His silence about well-known features of China makes some historians question how much he saw firsthand.

check.q: Which of these is an example of what both travelers left out?
choices: The daily lives of the poor and the enslaved
check.why: Both men wrote about courts, merchants and religion but said little about ordinary workers, women or enslaved people.

lessons.title: The Black Death
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1346 and 1351 a plague carried along trade routes killed roughly a third of the people of Europe and devastated the Middle East and North Africa.
reading: In October of 1347 a few Genoese trading ships pulled into the harbor of Messina, in Sicily. Most of the sailors were dead or dying. Swellings the size of eggs had appeared in their armpits and groins, followed by fever, black patches on the skin and death within days. The townspeople drove the ships away, but too late. Within months the disease was in every port of the Mediterranean.

The disease was *bubonic plague*, caused by a bacterium that lives in fleas carried by rats. It had probably started in Central Asia in the 1330s and moved along Mongol caravan routes to the Black Sea. From there Italian merchant ships carried it west. It hit the Middle East at the same time: Ibn Battuta saw it in Damascus in 1348, and Cairo, one of the world's largest cities, lost perhaps a third of its people. In Europe the plague spread from Italy to France, Spain, England and north to Scandinavia by 1350.

The numbers are staggering even as rough estimates. Historians think the *Black Death*, as later writers named it, killed somewhere between a third and a half of Europe's population, tens of millions of people, in about five years. Whole villages emptied. Florence, a city of perhaps ninety thousand, may have lost half its people. Priests died faster than others because they visited the sick. Chroniclers wrote of bodies stacked in trenches with no one left to ring the church bells.

People searched for causes and found the wrong ones. Doctors blamed bad air or the alignment of planets. Some blamed God's anger and marched through towns whipping themselves. Others blamed Jews and accused them of poisoning wells; in Strasbourg in 1349 the city's Jews were murdered on that false charge. The real cause, the bacterium Yersinia pestis, was not identified until 1894. The plague returned in waves for centuries, but nothing matched the first great wave.

words.d: a deadly disease caused by bacteria carried by fleas on rats; it produces swollen lumps called buboes
the name later given to the great plague that swept Eurasia and North Africa from about 1346 to 1351
an outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries or continents

look.title: A Writer Watches Florence Die
look.text: Giovanni Boccaccio, who lived through the plague in Florence, wrote that the disease was so terrifying that brothers abandoned brothers, wives left husbands, and even parents refused to tend their own sick children. He said the dead were carried out by paid porters and buried in trenches, packed in layers like cargo in a ship.
look.cite: Giovanni Boccaccio, introduction to the Decameron, Florence, about 1353 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Boccaccio wrote fiction as well as fact. What in this account could a historian check, and what would be hard to verify?

check.q: How did the plague travel from Central Asia to Europe?
choices: Through the air on desert winds
Along caravan routes to the Black Sea and then by ship
Carried by Mongol armies invading Italy
Through contaminated grain shipped from China
check.why: Fleas on rats moved with caravans across the Mongol network to Black Sea ports, and Italian merchant ships carried them west.

check.q: Roughly what share of Europe's population died in the first wave?
choices: Between a third and a half
check.why: Estimates vary, but historians agree the Black Death killed somewhere between a third and half of Europe's people in about five years.

check.q: Why did people in 1349 blame Jews for the plague?
choices: Jews were immune to the disease
Jewish merchants had brought the infected ships
Fear and old prejudice made a false accusation easy to believe
check.why: The well-poisoning charge had no basis. It grew from panic and existing hatred and led to massacres like the one in Strasbourg.

lessons.title: A World With Fewer People
lessons.mainIdea: The plague's death toll shifted power toward surviving workers, weakened serfdom in western Europe and shook people's faith in old authorities.
reading: Imagine a village where forty of every hundred people died in one summer. The fields are still there, but there are not enough hands to plow them. The lord who owns the land needs workers badly. The survivors know it. That is what happened across Europe after 1350, and it changed the balance of power between those who owned land and those who worked it.

Wages rose sharply because labor was scarce. Landlords tried to stop this. In England, Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers in 1351, which ordered workers to accept the wages paid before the plague. It largely failed; people simply moved to lords who paid more. *Serfdom*, the system that bound peasants to a lord's land, weakened in western Europe as peasants bargained for freedom or just walked away. When rulers pushed back with new taxes, peasants rebelled: in France in 1358 and in England in 1381.

The plague also shook belief in authority. Prayers had not stopped the dying; neither had doctors. Some people turned to intense personal religion, and images of dancing skeletons appeared on church walls. Others questioned the Church, which had lost many priests and replaced them with less-trained men. In the Middle East, the historian Ibn Khaldun, whose parents died of plague, wrote that it was as if the world had called out for oblivion and been answered.

Historians debate how much the plague explains. Some argue that fewer people meant more land, food and wages per person, and that this helped fuel the Renaissance and later exploration. Others point out that Egypt suffered similar losses without the same results. The disaster was the same; what people built afterward depended on the laws, land and institutions they already had.

words.d: a system in which peasants were bound to a lord's land and owed him labor; it weakened after the plague
a 1351 English law that tried and failed to freeze wages at pre-plague levels
a situation with too few workers for the work available, which pushes wages up

look.title: The Lord and the Plowman
look.text: A lord in England in 1352 has three hundred acres and half the workers he had four years ago. A plowman on his land has been offered double wages by a lord in the next valley. The law says the plowman must stay and take the old wage. The lord cannot afford to lose him, but he also cannot afford to pay double. Both of them know the law is hard to enforce.
look.prompt: What choices does each person have? Who holds more power now than before the plague, and why?

check.q: Why did wages rise after the Black Death?
choices: Fewer workers were available for the same amount of land
check.why: With a third or more of workers dead, landlords competed for the survivors, and competition pushed wages up.

check.q: What was the Statute of Labourers meant to do?
check.why: English landlords used Parliament in 1351 to try to freeze wages, but workers largely ignored it.

check.q: Why do historians compare Europe with Egypt after the plague?
choices: To show that similar losses led to different outcomes
To prove the plague started in Africa
check.why: Egypt lost as many people but did not see the same shifts. The comparison shows that existing institutions shaped what came next.

lessons.title: The Renaissance in Italy
lessons.mainIdea: In the wealthy city-states of Italy, scholars and artists revived ancient learning and turned their attention to the human world.
reading: Florence in 1400 was a city of bankers and cloth merchants. Its money came from wool, dye and loans to kings and popes. The Medici family alone had branches of their bank across Europe. Wealth like that bought more than palaces. It paid for tutors, libraries, sculptors and painters. Out of these Italian city-states came the movement historians call the *Renaissance*, a French word for rebirth, roughly from the 1300s to the 1500s.

What was reborn was ancient Greece and Rome. Scholars called *humanists* hunted through monastery libraries for lost Latin manuscripts and learned Greek to read Plato and Homer. When Constantinople was threatened and then fell in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Italy carrying more books. The humanists did not reject religion, but they argued that studying history, poetry and ethics could make a person wiser and better in this life, not only the next.

Artists caught the same spirit. In the early 1400s the architect Brunelleschi worked out the rules of *linear perspective*, a method for drawing so that objects shrink toward a vanishing point as they do to the eye. Painters used it to make flat walls open into believable rooms and landscapes. Brunelleschi also engineered the enormous brick dome of Florence's cathedral, finished in 1436, a feat no one had managed since ancient Rome. Leonardo da Vinci, born in 1452, filled notebooks with anatomy, machines and flowing water.

The Renaissance did not come from Italy alone. Many Greek works reached Europe through Arabic translations made in Baghdad and Spain centuries earlier. Paper came from China through the Muslim world. The gold that paid for Florence's art came partly from Mali. Seen from a distance, the rebirth of Europe was one more product of the networks this chapter has been tracing.

words.d: the rebirth of interest in ancient Greek and Roman learning and art in Europe, roughly 1300s to 1500s
a Renaissance scholar who studied ancient texts, history and ethics to understand human life
a drawing method in which lines converge on a vanishing point so a flat picture looks three-dimensional

look.title: Two Paintings of the Same Street
look.text: Picture two paintings side by side. In the older one, from around 1300, a city street is flat: the houses stack up like cards, people in the back are as large as those in front, and gold leaf fills the sky. In the newer one, from around 1450, the same street narrows toward a single point far away, the paving stones shrink with distance, and the sky is blue with clouds.
look.prompt: What does the newer painting suggest about what its artist and buyers valued? Why might a merchant city prefer it?

check.q: Where did the money for the Italian Renaissance mainly come from?
choices: Trade, banking and cloth manufacturing in city-states
check.why: Cities like Florence and Venice grew rich on trade and banking, and families like the Medici spent that wealth on art and learning.

check.q: What did humanists believe studying ancient texts could do?
choices: Make a person wiser and better in this life
check.why: Humanists valued history, poetry and ethics as guides to living well, without rejecting Christianity.

check.q: How did the wider world contribute to the Renaissance?
choices: Arabic translations, Chinese paper and African gold all flowed into Italy
check.why: Greek texts survived in Arabic, paper came from China via Muslim lands, and West African gold helped fund Italian wealth.

lessons.title: The Printing Press
lessons.mainIdea: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a press, and books became cheap enough to change who could read.
reading: Before 1450, every book in Europe was written by hand. A single Bible took a scribe about a year and cost as much as a house. Then, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg put together a new system. He cast individual letters in metal, arranged them in a frame, coated them with sticky oil-based ink, and pressed paper against them with a screw press adapted from wine making. His Bible, finished around 1455, was the first major book printed in Europe.

Gutenberg did not invent printing. Chinese printers had carved whole pages into wood blocks since the 800s, and Bi Sheng had made *movable type* from clay in the 1040s. Korean printers cast metal type and used it to print a Buddhist text in 1377. What was different in Europe was the alphabet. Chinese needs thousands of characters; Latin needs about two dozen letters. Movable type fit the alphabet perfectly, and Gutenberg's metal letters could be reused thousands of times.

The results came fast. By 1500, presses were running in more than two hundred European towns and had printed millions of books, more than all the scribes of the previous thousand years combined. Prices fell. Merchants bought manuals, students bought textbooks, and ordinary people bought pamphlets and prayer books in their own languages. Ideas that once took decades to spread now crossed Europe in months. Within seventy years the press would carry a religious revolt across the continent.

Printing also changed how people thought about truth. When every copy of a book is identical, readers in different cities can argue about the same page. Maps, star tables and anatomy drawings could be reproduced exactly instead of copied badly. Errors could be corrected in the next edition. Some historians argue that this fixed, shared knowledge made modern science possible.

words.d: individual letters or characters that can be arranged, inked, printed and then reused
a machine that presses inked type onto paper; Gutenberg's version appeared in Mainz around 1450
a person who copied books by hand before printing

look.title: Movable Type Across Eurasia
rows: Bi Sheng's clay movable type, China
Jikji printed with metal type, Korea
look.cite: Standard dates from surviving books and contemporary accounts
look.prompt: Movable type existed in Asia four centuries before Gutenberg. Why did it transform Europe faster than China? Think about alphabets.

check.q: Which of these did Gutenberg actually invent?
choices: None of these; he combined existing pieces into a new system
check.why: Printing, paper and movable type all existed earlier in Asia. Gutenberg's achievement was combining metal type, oil ink and a press.

check.q: Why did movable type suit Europe so well?
choices: The Latin alphabet has only about two dozen letters
Europeans had more paper than China
check.why: A small alphabet meant a printer needed only a few dozen kinds of type, reused endlessly, instead of thousands of characters.

check.q: How did printing help science, according to some historians?
choices: Identical copies let readers everywhere check and correct the same text
It ended the need for maps
check.why: Exact copies of tables, maps and drawings gave scholars a shared, fixed body of knowledge to build on and correct.

lessons.title: The Fall of Constantinople
lessons.mainIdea: In 1453 Ottoman cannon breached the walls of Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and reshaping trade and power in the eastern Mediterranean.
reading: For more than a thousand years, Constantinople had been the capital of the eastern Roman, or *Byzantine*, Empire. Its triple walls had turned back Persians, Arabs and Bulgars. By 1450 the empire behind those walls had shrunk to the city itself and a few scraps of land. Around it lay the growing empire of the *Ottoman Turks*, who had crossed from Asia into Europe a century earlier and were now ruled by a young sultan, Mehmed II.

In April 1453 Mehmed arrived with an army far larger than the defenders' and with something new: enormous bronze cannon, one so large it needed dozens of oxen to move. For weeks the guns pounded the ancient walls. When a chain across the harbor blocked his ships, Mehmed had them dragged overland on greased logs and launched into the water behind it. On May 29, after a siege of about fifty-three days, Ottoman soldiers broke through. The last Byzantine emperor died fighting. Mehmed rode into the great church of Hagia Sophia and turned it into a mosque.

The consequences rippled outward. The Ottomans now held the crossing between Europe and Asia and the sea route to the Black Sea. Italian merchants could still trade, but on Ottoman terms. Greek scholars carried manuscripts to Italy, feeding the Renaissance. And Europeans watched the lesson of the cannon closely: stone walls that had stood for centuries could now be knocked down in weeks. Every ruler who could afford it began buying guns.

Mehmed called himself Caesar and rebuilt the city, which came to be called Istanbul, as an imperial capital open to Muslims, Christians and Jews. Christian Europe called the fall a catastrophe; the Ottomans called it a conquest that God had promised. Both were describing the same day. A historian's job is to hold both views and explain what actually changed.

words.d: the eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, which lasted until 1453
a Muslim dynasty from Anatolia that built an empire across Southeast Europe, the Middle East and North Africa
surrounding a city or fortress to cut it off and force its surrender

look.title: Ships Over the Hill
look.text: Picture the night crews of Ottoman sailors and soldiers hauling dozens of ships out of the water, onto a road of greased timbers, and over a ridge into the harbor the Byzantines thought was safe. By morning the defenders on the sea walls saw an enemy fleet where there had been none. They had to spread their few soldiers even thinner.
look.prompt: Why was this move so effective? What does it show about the difference between having more soldiers and using them well?

check.q: What new technology was decisive in the siege of 1453?
check.why: Mehmed's giant guns battered walls that had resisted attackers for a thousand years.

check.q: How did the fall of Constantinople help the Renaissance?
choices: Greek scholars fled to Italy with ancient manuscripts
check.why: Refugee scholars brought Greek texts and language skills that Italian humanists were eager to learn.

check.q: Why did European rulers start buying cannon after 1453?
choices: The siege showed that old stone walls could no longer protect a city
The Ottomans sold them at a discount
Cannon were needed for religious ceremonies
check.why: Constantinople proved that gunpowder weapons could bring down even the strongest medieval walls.

lessons.title: Taking Stock in 1450
lessons.mainIdea: In 1450 no single region led the world; China, the Islamic lands, Europe and the Americas each had strengths the others lacked.
reading: Suppose you could stand above the Earth in 1450 and compare its regions. China under the Ming dynasty was the richest and most populous state, with printing, paper money, iron industry and the largest ships ever built. Yet in 1433 the Ming court had ended Zheng He's ocean voyages and turned its attention to the northern frontier. The Islamic world stretched across three continents, led in astronomy and medicine, and its Ottoman rulers had just shown the power of cannon.

Europe was, in most ways, a poorer and less advanced corner of Eurasia. It imported spices, silk and paper and paid for them with silver and African gold. But it was changing fast. Italian bankers had invented tools for moving money across borders. Gutenberg's press had just started running. Portuguese sailors, using compasses and lateen sails borrowed from Muslim seamen, had crept down the West African coast and reached the Senegal River by the mid-1440s in search of gold.

Across the Atlantic, peoples that Afro-Eurasia did not know existed had built their own civilizations. In central Mexico the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, on an island in a lake, was one of the largest cities in the world. In the Andes the Inca were building an empire linked by thousands of miles of stone roads. They had no iron, no horses, no wheeled vehicles and no immunity to Eurasian diseases. Those gaps would matter terribly within a century.

Why does this comparison matter? Because the story that follows, in which Europeans sailed across oceans and built empires, was not the result of Europe being ahead. In 1450 it was not. What Europe had was hunger for Asian goods, new guns and ships, competing kingdoms willing to gamble, and an Atlantic coastline facing the unknown. The next chapter follows what happened when those pieces met the winds.

words.d: the Chinese dynasty that ruled from 1368 to 1644 and sent, then ended, Zheng He's voyages
the Aztec capital, built on an island in a lake in central Mexico, one of the world's largest cities in 1450
the body's resistance to a disease, built up by past exposure over generations

look.title: Four Scholars, One Year
look.text: In 1450 a scholar in Nanjing reads a printed book that is centuries old. A scholar in Samarkand checks star tables at an observatory more accurate than any in Europe. A scholar in Florence copies a Greek manuscript by hand because printed copies do not yet exist. A scribe in Tenochtitlan paints a history in pictures on folded bark paper. None of them knows the other three exist.
look.prompt: Which of these four would have been most surprised by the world of 1550? Explain your reasoning.

check.why: Ming China had built Zheng He's giant fleet and had printed books for centuries, though it had just ended its ocean voyages.

choices: It was the wealthiest region on Earth
It was poorer than Asia but changing quickly
It had no contact with Africa or Asia

check.why: Europe imported Asian goods and lagged in many fields, but printing, banking and new ships were beginning to shift the balance.

check.q: What did the Aztec and Inca lack that would matter in the coming century?
choices: Iron, horses and immunity to Eurasian diseases
check.why: The Americas had complex states and huge cities but no iron tools, no horses and no exposure to diseases like smallpox.

review.q: What allowed Song China's population to grow so rapidly?
choices: Fast-ripening rice and two harvests a year
review.why: Champa rice let farmers grow more food, which supported a population of about one hundred million by the early 1100s.

review.q: Which invention reached the Islamic world from China and helped its scholarship flourish?
review.why: Paper mills in Samarkand and Baghdad made books cheap enough to fill libraries and madrasas.

review.q: What was the main purpose of the Mongol yam system?
choices: To speed messengers and travelers across the empire
review.why: Relay stations with fresh horses let messages and merchants cross Asia in a fraction of the usual time.

review.q: Why was the Indian Ocean easier to sail than the open Atlantic before 1500?
choices: The monsoon winds reversed predictably each season
review.why: Sailors could count on the summer and winter monsoons to carry them out and home on a known schedule.

review.q: What did Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage reveal about Mali?
choices: It was a poor desert kingdom
It controlled enormous quantities of gold
It had no contact with Islam
It was ruled by the Mongols
review.why: He gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value fell, and his fame reached European mapmakers.

review.why: Checking one source against independent evidence is corroboration, and it raises trust in the source.

review.q: Which was a long-term effect of the Black Death in western Europe?
review.why: With workers scarce, survivors bargained for higher pay and more freedom, and lords could not stop them.

review.q: What did Gutenberg's press and the fall of Constantinople have in common?
choices: Both were caused by the plague
Both showed new technology changing old ways around 1450
review.why: Movable type and heavy cannon each transformed something ancient: hand copying and stone walls.

chapters.title: The Atlantic World
chapters.bigQuestion: When the Atlantic became a highway instead of a wall, who gained, who lost, and how did one coin from Bolivia end up in China?

story.title: A Coin Crosses Two Oceans
story.kicker: In 1580 a silver coin dug from a mountain in the Andes could buy Chinese silk in Manila. Follow it and you follow the first truly global economy.
paragraphs: Start on a bare, freezing mountain in what is now Bolivia, more than thirteen thousand feet above the sea. The Spanish called it Cerro Rico, the Rich Hill. In 1545 silver was found there, and within a few decades the mining town of Potosí at its foot had grown into one of the largest cities in the world. Indigenous men, drafted under a labor system called the mita, climbed down ladders into the dark with candles tied to their foreheads and hauled out ore on their backs. Many did not come back up.

The ore was crushed and mixed with mercury to pull out the silver, then melted and struck into coins stamped with the Spanish king's arms. Each was a peso, a piece of eight. Mule trains carried the coins down to the Pacific coast. From there some went north to Panama, across the isthmus, and by ship to Spain, where the king used them to pay soldiers fighting in the Netherlands and Italy. But in 1580 a growing share went the other way.

That share was loaded at Acapulco onto a big-bellied Spanish ship called the Manila galleon. The galleon sailed west across the Pacific for two or three months to the Philippines, which Spain had claimed in 1565. Waiting in Manila were Chinese merchants from Fujian with silk, porcelain, lacquer and spices. They wanted one thing in return: silver. China's government had recently begun demanding that taxes be paid in silver, and the whole Ming economy was hungry for it.

So the coin from Potosí changed hands in Manila for a bolt of silk. The silk went back east on the galleon to Acapulco and Mexico City, where a Spanish official's wife wore it to Mass. The coin went to China, where it might be melted into an ingot or pass from hand to hand for a century. Historians estimate that a large share of all the silver mined in the Americas ended up in China. Chinese silk, Andean silver, Spanish ships, Filipino ports, Indigenous labor: one exchange, five continents.

This chapter is about how that world came to exist in barely a hundred years. It begins with the Portuguese feeling their way down the coast of Africa, follows Columbus into a sea he did not understand, and looks squarely at what the meeting of continents cost: empires destroyed, tens of millions dead of disease, and millions more carried in chains across the Atlantic. It ends with Europe itself split by religion and changed by new ways of knowing.
story.think: The silver in the coin was dug by Indigenous workers, minted by Spain, and spent in China. Who do you think benefited most from that coin, and who benefited least?

lessons.title: Portugal Learns the Atlantic
lessons.mainIdea: Portuguese sailors combined borrowed tools and new ships to work their way down Africa's coast and around it to India by 1498.
reading: Portugal is a small country on the western edge of Europe with its back to Spain and its face to the Atlantic. In the early 1400s its rulers had a problem and an idea. The problem was that Asian spices and African gold reached Europe through Muslim and Italian middlemen who took most of the profit. The idea was to sail around them. A prince later called Henry the Navigator, who died in 1460, sponsored voyage after voyage down the African coast.

The tools came from everywhere. The magnetic *compass* had reached Europe from China through the Islamic world. The *astrolabe*, refined by Muslim astronomers, let a sailor measure the height of the sun or a star and estimate his latitude. Arab lateen sails let a ship sail closer to the wind. Portuguese shipwrights combined them in the *caravel*, a small, fast, shallow ship that could explore rivers and coasts and, crucially, sail home against the wind.

Progress was slow and then sudden. Sailors feared the Atlantic's long westward loops of wind and current, but they learned to use them. By the 1440s the Portuguese had reached the Senegal River and were trading for gold and buying enslaved people. In 1482 they built a fort at Elmina, on the coast of modern Ghana, to guard the gold trade. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa. In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India and sailed home with spices worth many times the cost of his voyage.

One more piece of the story was planted on Atlantic islands. On Madeira and the Canaries, Portuguese and Spanish settlers grew sugar cane, a crop that needs heavy labor to cut and process. They used enslaved workers, at first from the Canaries and then from Africa. The island sugar plantation, worked by captives, was a small model of a system that would soon spread across the Atlantic on a vast and terrible scale.

a tool for measuring the height of the sun or stars to find a ship's latitude
a small, fast Portuguese ship with lateen sails that could sail against the wind

choices: None of these; all came from or through Asia and the Islamic world

A shortage of sugar in Europe

lessons.title: Columbus and the Taino
lessons.mainIdea: Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492 believing he was near Asia; for the Taino people who met him, the arrival began a catastrophe.
reading: Christopher Columbus was a sailor from Genoa who had studied the Portuguese voyages and drawn a wrong conclusion. He believed the Earth was much smaller than it is, so that Japan lay only a few thousand miles west of Spain. Educated people already knew the world was round; they doubted his distances, and they were right. After years of refusals, the rulers of Spain, Ferdinand and Isabella, agreed in 1492 to back him with three small ships.

On October 12, 1492, after about five weeks at sea, his crew sighted an island in the Bahamas. The people who lived there were *Taino*, farmers and fishers who grew cassava and corn and lived in villages under chiefs. Columbus wrote that they were generous, wore little gold, and would make good servants. He claimed their land for Spain, took several of them captive as interpreters and sailed on to Cuba and Hispaniola. He died in 1506 still insisting he had reached the edge of Asia.

Spain and Portugal quickly divided the world between them. In the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 they drew a line down the Atlantic: lands west of it would be Spain's, lands east Portugal's. No one asked the people living there. Spanish settlers on Hispaniola forced the Taino to dig for gold and grow food under a system called the *encomienda*, which gave a Spaniard the right to the labor of a group of Indigenous people in exchange for teaching them Christianity.

The result was collapse. Overwork, hunger, violence and above all diseases like smallpox, to which the Taino had no resistance, killed them by the tens of thousands. A Spanish priest, Bartolomé de las Casas, who had once held an encomienda himself, later wrote that of the hundreds of thousands living on Hispaniola in 1492, almost none were left within a few decades. His numbers are debated. The disappearance of a people is not.

words.d: the Indigenous people of the Caribbean islands whom Columbus met in 1492
a Spanish grant giving a settler the right to Indigenous people's labor in return for teaching them Christianity
the 1494 agreement in which Spain and Portugal divided the world along a line in the Atlantic

look.title: The First Day, in Columbus's Words
look.text: In his journal Columbus recorded that the islanders came out to the ships, traded parrots and cotton thread for glass beads and bells, and carried no weapons. He noted that they seemed quick to learn and that fifty men could subdue them all and make them do whatever was wanted.
look.cite: Christopher Columbus, journal of the first voyage, October 1492, as copied by Las Casas (paraphrased)
look.prompt: In the same entry Columbus admires the Taino and plans to subdue them. What does that tell you about how he saw the purpose of his voyage?

check.q: Why did educated people in Spain doubt Columbus's plan?
choices: They believed the Earth was flat
They thought Asia was much farther west than he claimed
They wanted to sail east instead
check.why: Scholars knew the Earth was round and roughly how big it was. Columbus had underestimated the distance, and they were right.

check.q: What was the encomienda?
choices: A treaty between Spain and Portugal
A grant of Indigenous labor to a Spanish settler
check.why: An encomienda gave a Spaniard control over the labor of a group of Indigenous people, supposedly in exchange for religious instruction.

check.q: What was the largest single cause of Taino deaths?
choices: Diseases to which they had no resistance
check.why: Overwork and violence killed many, but smallpox and other Eurasian diseases killed far more.

lessons.title: Why the Conquests Succeeded
lessons.mainIdea: Small Spanish forces toppled the Aztec and Inca empires because of disease, Indigenous allies, steel and horses, and timing, not because of Spanish courage alone.
reading: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with about five hundred men and a handful of horses. Two years later Tenochtitlan, a city of perhaps two hundred thousand people, lay in ruins and its ruler was dead. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than two hundred men, captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca and within a few years controlled an empire that stretched two thousand miles along the Andes. How could so few defeat so many?

The first answer is that they did not do it alone. The *Aztec* ruled by force over many peoples who paid them tribute and hated them. Cortés made allies of the Tlaxcalans, who sent tens of thousands of warriors against Tenochtitlan. Most of the army that took the city was Indigenous. In Peru, Pizarro arrived just after a civil war between two brothers for the Inca throne had torn the empire apart. He captured Atahualpa by treachery at a meeting, held him for a room full of gold, and then executed him.

The second answer is disease. Smallpox reached Mexico in 1520 with a Spanish expedition and swept through Tenochtitlan while it was under siege, killing the emperor Cuitlahuac and perhaps a large share of the city's people. It reached the Andes before Pizarro did, killing the Inca emperor Huayna Capac and setting off the civil war. An enemy that could not be seen did more to break these empires than any weapon.

Weapons did matter. Steel swords and armor, crossbows, a few cannon and above all horses gave Spanish soldiers advantages in open battle, since the Americas had no iron and no large riding animals. Cortés also had ships built to control the lake around Tenochtitlan. Yet the Aztec adapted quickly, and Indigenous accounts written in Nahuatl in the decades after describe fierce resistance, not a people paralyzed by awe. The conquests were real, but the reasons were more tangled than the conquerors' own stories claimed.

lessons.title: Crops and Animals Change Places
lessons.mainIdea: After 1492 plants and animals crossed the Atlantic in both directions and permanently changed what people ate and how they lived on every continent.
reading: Before 1492 no one in Italy had tasted a tomato. No one in Ireland had seen a potato. No one in India or Thailand had cooked with chili peppers. No horse had run on the Great Plains, and no cow, pig, sheep or chicken lived anywhere in the Americas. The two halves of the world had been separated for so long that they had grown different sets of plants, animals and germs. Historians call the swap that followed Columbus the *Columbian Exchange*.

From the Americas, Afro-Eurasia gained corn, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, peanuts, beans, squash, chili peppers, cacao, tobacco and pineapples. Some of these were more productive than any Old World crop. Potatoes could feed a family from a small plot and grew where wheat would not. Corn and sweet potatoes let Chinese farmers plant hillsides that had been useless for rice. Historians argue that these crops helped populations grow in Europe, China and West Africa in the centuries after 1600.

From Afro-Eurasia, the Americas gained wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, bananas, citrus fruit and, above all, animals. Horses transformed life for peoples of the Great Plains and the Argentine pampas, who became mounted hunters within a few generations. Cattle and pigs, running loose, multiplied into the millions. They also trampled Indigenous fields and spread across land that farmers had just been forced to abandon. The landscape itself changed.

The exchange was uneven in who chose it. European settlers brought their crops on purpose. Corn and potatoes crossed to Europe and Asia because farmers found them useful. But many exchanges were forced or accidental: African rice-growing skills traveled with enslaved people to the Carolinas, and earthworms, rats and weeds crossed in ships' ballast. The most consequential passengers of all, the germs, are the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.title: The Great Dying
lessons.mainIdea: Eurasian diseases killed the majority of the Indigenous population of the Americas within about a century, the largest demographic disaster in recorded history.
reading: In Afro-Eurasia, people had lived beside cattle, pigs and horses for thousands of years, and diseases had jumped from animals to humans: smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus. Those who survived childhood carried some resistance, and so did their children. The Americas had few domesticated animals and none of those diseases. When they arrived after 1492, they struck what historians call a *virgin soil epidemic*: a population in which no one had any immunity at all.

The results were unlike anything in the Old World, even the Black Death. Smallpox alone could kill half of a community in one pass. Measles, influenza and other illnesses followed, often in overlapping waves, so that survivors of one epidemic were weakened for the next. Farmers too sick to plant led to famine. Elders died before passing on knowledge. Populations that had never seen a European fell ill anyway, because the diseases traveled along Indigenous trade routes faster than the Spanish did.

The numbers are debated, because no one counted the population of the Americas in 1491. Estimates range from tens of millions to well over one hundred million. What most historians agree on is the scale of the fall: by about 1600 the Indigenous population had dropped by something like ninety percent. The Valley of Mexico, one of the most densely populated places on Earth, lost the great majority of its people within eighty years of Cortés's arrival.

We know this partly from Spanish tax counts, which shrank decade by decade. We also know it from Indigenous voices. In the 1570s, Nahua scholars worked with the Spanish priest Bernardino de Sahagún to record, in their own language, what the 1520 smallpox had been like. They described sores that covered people from head to foot. They described the sick who could not move or turn over. They described the many who starved because no one was left to care for them. It is one of the few disasters this large described by the people who lived it.

lessons.title: Silver and the First Global Trade
lessons.mainIdea: Silver from Potosí and Mexico, mined with forced labor, flowed to Spain and to China and tied the world's economies together for the first time.
reading: Potosí, the silver mountain in the Andes, was discovered in 1545. By 1600 the town beneath it had swelled to perhaps one hundred fifty thousand people, larger than any city in Spain. The Spanish crown took a fifth of every bar of silver as tax. To keep the ore flowing, the viceroy revived the Inca system of labor draft, the *mita*, and required Indigenous villages across the region to send one seventh of their men to the mines each year. The work was brutal, and mercury used to refine the ore poisoned workers slowly.

The silver went two ways. Fleets carried it across the Atlantic to Seville, where it paid for Spain's wars and drained away to bankers in Genoa and Antwerp who had lent the king money. So much silver arrived that prices across Europe rose for a century, a slow *inflation* that hurt people on fixed incomes and helped merchants. Spain's kings spent the money as fast as it came and went bankrupt several times anyway.

The other route was across the Pacific. Beginning in 1571, Spanish galleons sailed each year between Acapulco in Mexico and Manila in the Philippines. There Chinese traders exchanged silk and porcelain for silver. China had a huge economy and little silver of its own, and in the 1570s the Ming government began requiring taxes to be paid in silver. So silver was worth more in China than anywhere else, and merchants bought it there with goods. Historians estimate that a large share of American silver ended up in China, some by way of Europe and India.

This was the first time a single commodity linked every inhabited continent. A drought at Potosí could raise prices in Fujian. A Ming tax reform could change the fortunes of miners in the Andes. Money, in the form of the Spanish peso, became the closest thing to a world currency; it was legal tender in the United States until the 1850s. And all of it rested on the men who climbed down into the Rich Hill by candlelight.

lessons.title: The Transatlantic Slave Trade
lessons.mainIdea: Over about 350 years, roughly twelve and a half million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas, most to work sugar and other plantations.
reading: Sugar started it. Europeans wanted sugar, sugar cane grew well in the Caribbean and Brazil, and the Indigenous people who might have been forced to grow it were dying of disease. Portuguese traders already bought captives on the African coast. Beginning in the early 1500s and growing every decade, European ships carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Historians using surviving ship records count roughly twelve and a half million people forced aboard between about 1500 and 1866, of whom about ten and a half million survived the crossing.

The system worked as a triangle. Ships from Europe carried cloth, guns, iron and rum to West Africa. There, at forts like Elmina and ports like Ouidah, they traded these goods to African merchants and rulers for captives, who had usually been taken in wars or raids inland. The ships then crossed the Atlantic on the *Middle Passage*, a voyage of one to three months in which people were chained below decks in heat, filth and disease. Roughly one in seven died at sea. In the Americas the survivors were sold, and the ships loaded sugar, tobacco or silver for Europe.

Slavery had existed in Africa, Europe and Asia for thousands of years, but this system was new in three ways. Its scale was vast. It was *chattel slavery*, meaning people were treated as property that could be bought, sold, mortgaged and inherited, and their children were born enslaved. And it was tied to race: over time, laws in the Americas defined enslavement as a condition for people of African descent alone. That link between skin color and slavery was built, deliberately, in these centuries.

Who was responsible? European merchants and governments organized and profited from the trade. So did African rulers and traders who sold captives, sometimes under pressure, sometimes eagerly, and some kingdoms grew powerful on guns bought with human beings. Plantation owners in the Americas demanded ever more workers. Consumers in Europe bought the sugar. The evidence points not at one villain but at a system in which many people found it profitable to look away.

lessons.title: Resistance and Survival
lessons.mainIdea: Africans resisted enslavement at every stage, from kings who protested to captives who revolted at sea and communities of escapees who fought colonial armies.
reading: Resistance began in Africa. In 1526 Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, wrote to the king of Portugal complaining that Portuguese traders were kidnapping his people, even nobles and relatives of his own family, and carrying them off to be sold. He asked that the trade be stopped. It was not. A century later Queen Nzinga of Ndongo, in what is now Angola, fought the Portuguese for decades, making alliances, leading troops and negotiating until her death in 1663.

On the ships, captives rose up whenever they could. Records show revolts on roughly one in ten slaving voyages, which is why crews kept men chained and mounted guns facing the deck. Some captives refused food. Some jumped overboard. The cost of guarding against rebellion was so high that historians think it reduced the total number of people carried by hundreds of thousands. Every revolt made the trade a little more expensive, and expense was the only argument the traders understood.

In the Americas, enslaved people escaped when they could and built free communities in mountains and swamps. Colonists called them *maroons*. In Brazil, escapees founded Palmares, a settlement of thousands that survived Portuguese attacks for most of the 1600s before it was destroyed in 1694. In Jamaica, Mexico, Colombia and Suriname, maroon communities fought colonial troops to a standstill and in some cases forced treaties recognizing their freedom.

Most people could not escape, and their resistance took quieter forms. They worked slowly, broke tools, kept their languages and religions alive, and raised children with memories of Africa. West African rice farming techniques, music, foods and beliefs survived and reshaped the cultures of Brazil, the Caribbean and the American South. Survival itself, under a system built to erase people, was a form of resistance, and historians now read the evidence for it as carefully as they read the ship logs.

lessons.title: The Reformation
lessons.mainIdea: Beginning in 1517, Martin Luther's protest split Western Christianity, and the printing press turned a local argument into a continental revolt.
reading: In 1517 a monk and professor named Martin Luther, in the small German town of Wittenberg, was angry about *indulgences*. The Church was selling certificates that promised to reduce punishment for sins in the afterlife, and the money was going to build St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Luther wrote ninety-five arguments against the practice, in Latin, for scholars to debate. Within weeks printers had translated and reprinted them. Within months they were being read across Germany.

Luther's ideas went far beyond indulgences. He argued that people are saved by faith alone, not by good works or Church rituals, and that the Bible, not the pope, was the final authority. He translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it. When the pope excommunicated him in 1521 and the emperor ordered him arrested, German princes protected him, partly from conviction and partly because breaking with Rome let them seize Church lands. The movement became known as the *Reformation*, and its followers as Protestants.

The split spread and multiplied. In Switzerland, John Calvin built a strict Protestant community in Geneva and sent trained preachers across Europe. In England, King Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 mainly to end his marriage, and made himself head of the English church. The Catholic Church answered with its own reform: the Council of Trent, from 1545 to 1563, clarified doctrine and cleaned up abuses, and a new order, the Jesuits, founded schools and sent missionaries from Brazil to Japan.

Religion and politics could not be pulled apart, and the result was war. France was torn by decades of fighting between Catholics and Protestants, including the massacre of thousands of Protestants in Paris in 1572. The Thirty Years' War, from 1618 to 1648, drew in most of Europe and devastated Germany, where some regions lost a third or more of their people. The Peace of Westphalia that ended it let each ruler choose the religion of his state. Europe would remain divided, and rulers learned that armies, not sermons, settled the question.

lessons.title: The Scientific Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: Between about 1543 and 1687, European thinkers replaced ancient authority with observation, measurement and mathematics as the way to know how nature works.
reading: For fourteen hundred years, educated people in Europe and the Islamic world had agreed on one picture of the heavens. The Earth sat still at the center of the universe. The sun, planets and stars moved around it. It matched what the eye saw and what ancient Greek authorities and the Church taught. In 1543 a Polish churchman, Nicolaus Copernicus, published a book arguing the opposite: the sun was at the center and the Earth was a planet moving around it. He waited until he was dying to publish, and few people at first believed him.

The next generation supplied the evidence. The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe measured the positions of planets more precisely than anyone before. His assistant Johannes Kepler used those numbers to show that planets move in ellipses, not perfect circles, following exact mathematical laws. In 1609 the Italian Galileo Galilei built a *telescope* and turned it on the sky. He saw mountains on the moon, moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus, none of which fit the old picture. He published quickly, in Italian as well as Latin, and printing carried his drawings across Europe.

Authority pushed back. In 1633 the Church put Galileo on trial and forced him to deny that the Earth moves; he spent his last years under house arrest. Yet the method he used spread anyway: observe carefully, measure, test ideas against evidence, and describe results in mathematics. Thinkers called it the *scientific method*. In 1687 the Englishman Isaac Newton showed that a single law of gravity explained both a falling apple and the orbit of the moon. The universe, it seemed, ran on laws that human reason could discover.

This *Scientific Revolution* did not happen in a vacuum. Copernicus used mathematical tools developed by astronomers in the Islamic world. Printing let scientists compare identical tables and correct each other. Voyages across oceans had already shown that ancient geographers were wrong about the world, which made people readier to doubt them about the heavens. And the new confidence that nature followed discoverable laws would soon be turned on government and society, as the next chapter shows.
