lessons.title: One Connected World
lessons.mainIdea: By 1650 Europeans, Africans and Indigenous Americans lived, worked and mixed in a single Atlantic world whose trade and people reached across the Pacific to Asia.
reading: Walk through Mexico City in 1650 and you would hear Spanish, Nahuatl and African languages in the same market. Spanish officials, Indigenous farmers, enslaved and free Africans, and people of mixed descent bought chocolate, wheat bread, Chinese silk and cotton cloth from India. Colonial artists painted series of portraits classifying families by ancestry, a sign of how much mixing had happened and how anxious the rulers were to rank it. This was a new kind of society, born of the exchange.

The Atlantic was now crossed constantly. Sugar from Brazil and the Caribbean went to Europe; cloth and guns went to Africa; captives went to the Americas; silver went everywhere. In 1602 the Dutch founded the East India Company, the first business to sell shares to the public, and its ships soon dominated the spice trade in Asia. Amsterdam replaced Antwerp and Seville as Europe's money center. Rivalry among European powers over this trade produced wars that were fought on four continents.

Indigenous peoples did not simply vanish. In Mexico and the Andes, communities survived, kept their languages, went to court against Spanish landowners and rebuilt after the epidemics. In North America, the Iroquois, Algonquian and other nations traded furs with the French, Dutch and English, played rivals against each other and shaped how colonies grew. Africans and their descendants built churches, brotherhoods and free towns. The world of 1650 was made by all of them, not only by Europeans.

So who gained and who lost? Europe gained new lands, crops, silver and eventually the wealth that would help fuel its later rise. China gained silver and new food crops. Africa lost millions of people and saw some states corrupted by the trade in captives. Indigenous America lost most of its people and its independence. A student in Illinois today eats corn from the Americas, wheat from Eurasia and chocolate sweetened with sugar first grown by enslaved labor. The Atlantic world is not history that ended; it is the ground we stand on.

chapters.title: Empires and the State
chapters.bigQuestion: Between 1500 and 1750 rulers from Istanbul to Edo built stronger states than ever before. What did that power rest on, and why did some of it last while some crumbled?

story.title: The Emperor Who Wanted to Hear Everyone
story.kicker: In the 1570s the most powerful ruler in India built a hall where Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Christians argued about God while he listened.
paragraphs: Akbar became emperor of Mughal India in 1556, at the age of thirteen. His grandfather Babur had swept down from Central Asia and conquered Delhi in 1526. Akbar spent his first twenty years as ruler fighting to hold and enlarge that conquest, until his empire stretched across most of northern India. He could not read; he had tutors read to him for hours. And he ruled a land where most of his subjects were Hindus and he and his soldiers were Muslims.

In 1575, in his new red sandstone capital at Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar built a House of Worship. On Thursday evenings he gathered scholars there to debate. At first only Muslims came, and their arguments turned into shouting. So Akbar widened the circle. He invited Hindu pandits, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests from Gujarat, and, in 1580, Jesuit priests from the Portuguese colony of Goa, who hoped to convert him. He sat among them, asked questions, and let each side attack the others' beliefs.

Some of the courtiers were appalled. A Muslim historian at the court later wrote bitterly that the emperor had lost his faith and let unbelievers insult the Prophet. The Jesuits went home disappointed that Akbar never became a Christian. Akbar himself drew his own conclusions. He had already abolished the special tax that Muslim rulers charged non-Muslims. He married Hindu princesses and let them keep their religion. He appointed Hindu nobles to high office and had Hindu epics translated into Persian.

Akbar's chief minister called this policy universal peace: the idea that the ruler should stand above the quarrels of faiths and protect them all. Was it belief or strategy? Probably both. A Muslim minority could not hold India by force alone; it needed Hindu warriors, bankers and farmers to accept its rule. Tolerance was a way of governing as well as a conviction. A century later Akbar's great-grandson Aurangzeb would reverse it, restore the tax, and find his empire harder to hold.

This chapter is about rulers like Akbar and the states they built: the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals with their gunpowder armies, the Ming and Qing in China, the shoguns who sealed Japan, Peter who dragged Russia toward Europe, Louis XIV who made himself the sun of France, and the English who beheaded one king and fired another. It asks what each state rested on, how they paid for their armies, and why thinkers of the 1700s began to argue that power belonged to the people instead.
story.think: Akbar's tolerance was both a belief and a way to keep power. Can you think of a policy today that leaders support for both reasons at once?

lessons.title: The Ottomans at Their Height
lessons.mainIdea: Under Suleiman in the mid-1500s the Ottoman Empire ruled three continents through a disciplined slave army, a professional bureaucracy and a policy of governing non-Muslims through their own communities.
reading: By 1550 the Ottoman sultan ruled from Hungary to Iraq and from the Black Sea to Algeria. Suleiman, who reigned from 1520 to 1566, was called the Magnificent by Europeans and the Lawgiver by his own people. He had besieged Vienna in 1529 and nearly taken it. His navy controlled most of the Mediterranean. His empire, with Istanbul at its heart, was the largest and richest in Europe and the Middle East, and it was built on gunpowder.

Historians call the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals the *gunpowder empires* because cannon and muskets let them crush older armies and knock down old walls. The Ottoman core was the *janissaries*, infantry armed with muskets. They were recruited through the devshirme, a levy that took Christian boys from the Balkans, converted them to Islam, and trained them as soldiers or officials owing loyalty to the sultan alone. Some rose to be grand vizier, the empire's chief minister. It was a strange kind of slavery that could lead to the top of the state.

Ruling so many peoples required flexibility. Most Ottoman subjects in Europe were Christians; many in cities were Jews who had fled Spain after 1492. The empire organized them into communities called *millets*, each led by its own religious leaders, keeping its own courts and schools, and paying a special tax. It was not equality: non-Muslims had fewer rights. But it was far more tolerance than Christian Europe offered to Muslims or Jews at the time.

How do we know what the Ottoman state looked like from the inside? Its bureaucrats kept enormous registers of villages, taxes and soldiers that still fill archives in Istanbul. Foreign ambassadors wrote detailed reports home. One Habsburg envoy in the 1550s marveled that Ottoman officials rose by ability rather than birth, and warned that his own side, which gave commands to well-born amateurs, would lose. He was describing the empire at its peak; the next two centuries would test it.

words.d: a state of the 1500s and 1600s, like the Ottoman, Safavid or Mughal, built on armies armed with cannon and muskets
an Ottoman infantry soldier, usually recruited as a boy from Christian families and trained to serve the sultan
a religious community in the Ottoman Empire that governed its own members' religious and legal affairs
a high minister in a Muslim state; the grand vizier was the sultan's chief minister

look.title: An Enemy's Admiration
look.text: The Habsburg ambassador wrote that no Ottoman official held rank because of his birth. Each man's honor came from his own merit and service, and the sultan gave posts to those with ability, not to those with famous ancestors. He warned that Europe, which handed commands to nobles by birth, could not match such a system.
look.cite: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, Habsburg ambassador to Suleiman, letters written in the 1550s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Busbecq was an enemy of the Ottomans. Does that make his praise more or less believable? What might he have wanted his readers at home to do?

check.q: Why are the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals called gunpowder empires?
choices: Cannon and muskets let them defeat older armies and fortresses
Their capitals were built near gunpowder mines
check.why: All three rose by using firearms and artillery effectively against rivals who lacked them or used them less well.

check.q: How were janissaries recruited?
choices: Taken as boys from Christian families, converted and trained
check.why: The devshirme levy took Christian boys, mostly from the Balkans, and raised them as soldiers or officials loyal only to the sultan.

check.q: What was the millet system?
choices: A way of choosing the grand vizier
Letting each religious community govern its own affairs under its own leaders
check.why: Christians and Jews kept their own courts and schools and paid a special tax; they had fewer rights but more tolerance than minorities in Europe.

lessons.title: Safavid Persia and Its Rival
lessons.mainIdea: The Safavids made Shia Islam the religion of Persia, fought the Sunni Ottomans for two centuries, and under Shah Abbas built Isfahan into one of the world's great cities.
reading: In 1501 a fourteen-year-old named Ismail, leader of a religious brotherhood, took the city of Tabriz and declared himself shah of Persia. He did something that shaped the Middle East to this day: he made *Shia Islam* the official religion of his state. Shia Muslims believe that leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to the Prophet's son-in-law Ali and his descendants; *Sunni* Muslims, the majority worldwide, do not. Persia had been mostly Sunni. Ismail's Safavid dynasty forced the change, and Iran has been mostly Shia ever since.

The Ottomans, who were Sunni, saw the new Shia state on their border as both a rival and a heresy. In 1514 at Chaldiran, Ottoman cannon and muskets destroyed Ismail's cavalry, which had charged with swords. The lesson was brutal and clear: an empire without gunpowder could not survive. The two empires fought on and off for two hundred years, and the border they eventually settled on runs close to the modern border between Turkey and Iran. Religious difference and imperial rivalry reinforced each other.

The greatest Safavid ruler, Shah Abbas, reigned from 1588 to 1629. He rebuilt the army with muskets and cannon, using enslaved soldiers from the Caucasus much as the Ottomans used janissaries. He moved the capital to *Isfahan* and made it a showpiece: an enormous central square, a bazaar, a blue-tiled royal mosque and gardens. He welcomed Armenian Christian merchants, moving thousands of them to a suburb of the city, because they ran the silk trade with Europe and India that paid for his state.

Isfahan was so grand that Persians said it was half the world. English and Dutch trading companies opened offices there. Yet the Safavid state depended heavily on the shah himself. After Abbas, weaker rulers let the army decay and the treasury empty. In 1722 an army of Afghan rebels captured Isfahan and the dynasty collapsed. Its religious legacy outlasted its political one by centuries.

words.d: the branch of Islam holding that leadership should have passed to Ali and his descendants; made Persia's state religion in 1501
the larger branch of Islam, which accepted the early caliphs as rightful leaders; the Ottomans were Sunni
the Safavid capital rebuilt by Shah Abbas around 1600, famous for its great square and tiled mosques

look.title: The Square at Isfahan
look.text: Stand in the middle of Isfahan's great square around 1620. On one side rises the royal mosque with its blue-tiled dome. Opposite it is the gate of the bazaar, where merchants sell silk, carpets and Chinese porcelain. On a third side stands the shah's palace with a high balcony from which he watches polo matches played on the square itself. Armenian traders, Indian bankers and Dutch agents cross the square on business.
look.prompt: Religion, trade and royal power face each other across one square. What does that layout say about how Shah Abbas wanted his state to be seen?

check.q: What lasting change did Shah Ismail make in 1501?
choices: He made Shia Islam the official religion of Persia
He made Persia part of the Ottoman Empire
check.why: Ismail imposed Shia Islam on a mostly Sunni population, and Iran has remained largely Shia to this day.

check.q: What did the battle of Chaldiran in 1514 show?
choices: That Persia could defeat the Ottomans
That an army without gunpowder could not compete
That religion did not matter in war
check.why: Ottoman cannon and muskets shattered the Safavid cavalry charge, forcing later shahs to build gunpowder armies.

check.q: Why did Shah Abbas settle Armenian Christians in Isfahan?
choices: Because they ran the silk trade that funded his state
check.why: Armenian merchants had the networks to sell Persian silk to Europe and India, bringing in the money the state needed.

lessons.title: The Mughals from Akbar to Aurangzeb
lessons.mainIdea: The Mughals ruled most of India for two centuries by combining military power, an efficient land tax and, under Akbar, religious tolerance that later rulers abandoned.
reading: In 1526 Babur, a prince descended from both Genghis Khan and Timur, defeated the sultan of Delhi with cannon and muskets at Panipat. His grandson Akbar, who reigned from 1556 to 1605, turned the conquest into an empire. Akbar's genius was organization. He divided the empire into provinces run by paid officials. He had every field measured and its usual yield recorded, then set a land tax at a fixed share of the crop, collected in cash. This *land revenue* system gave the Mughals a steady income far larger than any European king's.

Akbar also built a system of ranks called *mansabdars*: every noble held a number that fixed his salary and how many cavalry he had to supply. Ranks were not inherited, and when a noble died his property returned to the emperor. This kept the nobility dependent and the army large. Hindu Rajput warriors were given high ranks and married into the royal family. Akbar abolished the *jizya*, the tax on non-Muslims, in 1564, and welcomed all faiths at court.

His descendants inherited great wealth. Shah Jahan, who reigned from 1628 to 1658, built the Taj Mahal at Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal; it took more than twenty years and thousands of workers. Mughal India in the 1600s produced perhaps a quarter of the world's manufactured goods, above all cotton cloth, and sold it to Asia, Africa and Europe. The Dutch and English East India Companies begged for permission to trade at Mughal ports.

Shah Jahan's son Aurangzeb, who reigned from 1658 to 1707, spent decades at war in the south and reversed Akbar's policy. He restored the jizya in 1679, destroyed some Hindu temples and enforced strict Islamic law. Whether this or the endless wars did more damage, historians argue. What is clear is that revolts by Marathas, Sikhs and Rajputs multiplied. After Aurangzeb's death the empire fragmented, and by the 1740s the emperor in Delhi ruled little beyond the city.

words.d: the Mughal tax on farmland, set as a fixed share of the usual crop and paid in cash
a Mughal noble holding a numbered rank that set his pay and the number of cavalry he had to supply
a tax charged to non-Muslims in many Islamic states; Akbar abolished it in 1564 and Aurangzeb restored it in 1679

look.title: Peace With All
look.text: Akbar's minister and historian Abul Fazl wrote that the emperor followed a policy of universal peace, treating all his subjects alike whatever their religion, and that a ruler who let religious hatred divide his people had failed in his duty to God, who had made all of them.
look.cite: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, court history of Akbar's reign, 1590s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Abul Fazl was Akbar's employee and admirer. How should that shape the way you use his account of the emperor's motives?

check.q: What gave the Mughal emperors an income far larger than European kings had?
choices: A land tax based on measured fields and recorded yields
Fees paid by European trading companies
The sale of cotton cloth by the emperor himself
check.why: Akbar's officials measured every field and set a cash tax on its usual crop, producing a huge, steady revenue.

check.q: Why did Mughal ranks not pass from father to son?
choices: The emperor did not want a hereditary nobility that could challenge him
The ranks were sold at auction
check.why: By taking back a noble's property at death and reassigning ranks, the emperor kept nobles dependent on him.

check.q: Which of these did Aurangzeb do?
choices: Restored the jizya and enforced strict Islamic law
check.why: Aurangzeb reversed Akbar's tolerance, restoring the tax on non-Muslims in 1679; Akbar had abolished it and Shah Jahan built the Taj.

lessons.title: Ming to Qing China
lessons.mainIdea: In 1644 the Manchus replaced the Ming and built the Qing, the largest Chinese empire ever, while keeping most of China's traditional government.
reading: The Ming dynasty had ruled China since 1368. By the early 1600s it was in trouble. Silver imports fell, taxes rose, harvests failed in a cold spell, and peasants rebelled. In 1644 a rebel army took Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. A Ming general then made a fateful choice: he opened the gate in the Great Wall to the *Manchus*, a people from the northeast, to help crush the rebels. The Manchus crushed them and stayed. Their dynasty, the *Qing*, ruled China until 1912.

The Manchus were a tiny minority ruling a vast population. They kept themselves separate, organized under military units called banners, and forbade intermarriage with Chinese. They ordered every Chinese man to shave his forehead and wear his hair in a long braid, the *queue*, as a sign of submission. But they also kept the Ming system almost intact: the civil service exams, the Confucian officials, the same ministries. Two great emperors, Kangxi and his grandson Qianlong, between them ruled for more than a century.

Under the Qing, China roughly doubled in size. Armies conquered Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and the far western region of Xinjiang. Population grew fast, from perhaps one hundred fifty million to more than three hundred million by 1800, fed partly by corn and sweet potatoes from the Americas. Kangxi welcomed Jesuit missionaries at court for their skill in astronomy, mapmaking and cannon casting, though few Chinese converted. Silver from the Americas kept flowing in to pay for tea, silk and porcelain.

The Qing were confident, and they had reason to be. In 1757 the court limited European traders to the single port of Canton, dealing through licensed Chinese merchants. It was not that China feared Europe; it was that China did not much need it. A British visitor in the 1790s would be told that the empire possessed all things and had no use for foreign manufactures. That confidence would look different a century later, but in 1750 it was hard to argue with.

words.d: a people from northeast of the Great Wall who conquered China in 1644 and founded the Qing dynasty
the Manchu dynasty that ruled China from 1644 to 1912 and expanded it to its largest size
the shaved forehead and long braid that Qing rulers required Chinese men to wear as a sign of submission

look.title: A Jesuit at the Emperor's Table
look.text: Picture a Jesuit priest from France in the 1690s, dressed in Chinese silk robes, kneeling before the Kangxi emperor with a set of instruments for measuring the stars. The emperor questions him closely about geometry and then asks him to help correct the calendar. The priest has spent years learning Chinese and hopes the emperor will convert. The emperor hopes the priest will cast better cannon.
look.prompt: Each man wants something from the other. Who is getting the better deal, and what does the scene tell you about how the Qing saw European knowledge?

check.q: How did the Manchus get inside the Great Wall in 1644?
choices: A Ming general opened the gate to get their help against rebels
The wall had never been finished
They bribed the last Ming emperor
check.why: With Beijing fallen to rebels, a Ming general let the Manchu army through to restore order; they then took power themselves.

check.q: Which of these did the Qing change?
check.why: The Qing kept the exams, ministries and Beijing as capital but forced Chinese men to wear the queue as a sign of submission.

check.q: Why did the Qing limit European trade to Canton in 1757?
choices: They had lost a war to Britain
They felt they had little need for European goods and wanted to control the trade
check.why: China was confident and largely self-sufficient, so the court kept foreign traders in one port under licensed Chinese merchants.

lessons.title: Tokugawa Japan Closes Its Doors
lessons.mainIdea: After 1600 the Tokugawa shoguns ended a century of civil war, controlled the warrior lords tightly, and sealed Japan off from almost all foreign contact for more than two centuries.
reading: In 1600, at the battle of Sekigahara, a warlord named Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated his rivals and ended more than a century of civil war among Japan's feudal lords, the *daimyo*. In 1603 the emperor, who reigned but did not rule, named him *shogun*, supreme military commander. Ieyasu built his capital at Edo, the fishing village that became Tokyo. His family would hold the office of shogun for more than 250 years.

The Tokugawa kept the peace by controlling the daimyo. Each lord ruled his own domain but had to spend every other year in Edo and leave his wife and children there permanently when he went home. This system, called *alternate attendance*, kept the lords under the shogun's eye, and the cost of keeping two households and traveling with a large escort drained their treasuries. Roads, inns and towns grew up along the routes. Edo became one of the largest cities in the world, with about a million people by the 1700s.

Foreigners were the other threat. Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries had arrived in the 1540s, bringing muskets and Christianity, and by 1600 there may have been three hundred thousand Japanese Christians. The shoguns feared that Christian daimyo might ally with European powers. They banned Christianity in 1614, executed missionaries and converts, and crushed a rebellion of Christian peasants in 1638. In the 1630s a series of edicts forbade Japanese to leave the country or return, and expelled almost all Europeans.

The policy is called *sakoku*, the closed country, though the door was never fully shut. Dutch traders were allowed one tiny artificial island in Nagasaki harbor, and Chinese and Korean merchants also traded under strict rules. Through that Dutch window, Japanese scholars studied European medicine, astronomy and guns in what they called Dutch learning. Japan enjoyed two centuries of peace, growing cities, printed books and popular theater. It also missed much of what was happening in the world, a gap it would have to close in a hurry after 1853.

words.d: a Japanese feudal lord who ruled a domain and commanded samurai warriors
Japan's supreme military ruler, who governed in the emperor's name from 1603 to 1868
the Tokugawa rule that daimyo spend every other year in Edo and leave their families there as hostages
the closed-country policy of the 1630s that banned Japanese from leaving and expelled most foreigners

look.title: The Closed Country Edict
look.text: The shogun's orders of 1635 declared that no Japanese ship or person might leave for a foreign country. Anyone who secretly went abroad would be executed, and any Japanese who had lived overseas and returned would be put to death. Officials were to search arriving ships for Christian priests, and anyone who reported a hidden priest would be rewarded.
look.cite: Tokugawa edict on foreign travel and Christianity, 1635 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The edict pairs foreign travel with Christianity as dangers. Why might a government see those two things as the same threat?

check.q: Who held real power in Tokugawa Japan?
check.why: The emperor reigned as a symbol, but the shogun commanded the armies and governed the country.

check.q: How did alternate attendance weaken the daimyo?
choices: It kept them under watch in Edo and drained their money on travel and two households
It forced them to become Christians
It required them to fight the Dutch
check.why: Living half the time in Edo, with families held there, the lords could not plot easily and spent heavily on the journeys.

check.q: Why was Japan never completely closed under sakoku?
choices: Japanese merchants traded freely in China
Dutch, Chinese and Korean traders were allowed under strict limits
check.why: A Dutch post at Nagasaki and Chinese and Korean trade kept a narrow channel open through which some foreign knowledge entered.

lessons.title: Russia Under Peter
lessons.mainIdea: Peter the Great forced Russia to copy European armies, navies and customs, built a new capital on the Baltic, and made the tsar's power more absolute than ever.
reading: In 1697 a very tall young man traveling under a false name turned up in a Dutch shipyard and asked for work as a carpenter. He was Peter, tsar of Russia, on a tour of Western Europe to learn how it built ships, cast cannon and ran governments. Russia was huge, mostly peasant, and cut off from Europe's seas and ideas. Peter had decided to change that by force. He reigned from 1682 to 1725, and by the end no one could doubt he had.

He started with symbols. Returning home, he ordered nobles to shave their beards and wear Western clothes, and taxed those who refused. He moved the calendar and the alphabet closer to Europe's. Then he built substance. He created a navy from nothing, founded schools of navigation and engineering, and replaced the old nobility of birth with a *Table of Ranks* in 1722 that tied noble status to service in the army or government. A commoner who rose through the ranks became a noble; a noble who did not serve lost his standing.

Peter's obsession was a port on the Baltic Sea, which Sweden controlled. The Great Northern War lasted from 1700 to 1721. After early defeats, Peter rebuilt his army with muskets, drill and cannon cast from church bells, and crushed the Swedes at Poltava in 1709. On marshy land captured from Sweden he built a new capital, *St. Petersburg*, laid out on European lines with canals and palaces. Tens of thousands of forced laborers died building it. He called it his window on Europe.

The cost fell on ordinary Russians. Taxes rose steeply, and Peter tightened *serfdom* so that landlords could buy and sell peasants and the state could draft them for twenty-five years in the army. Russia became a great European power, but it did so by strengthening the two things that Western Europe was starting to weaken: the absolute power of the ruler and the bondage of the peasants. That contradiction would shape Russia for two hundred years.

words.d: the title of the Russian emperor, from the Latin Caesar
Peter's 1722 system that tied noble status to service in the army or government instead of birth
the capital Peter built on the Baltic coast beginning in 1703 as his window on Europe
a system binding peasants to the land and their lord; Peter made it harsher in Russia

look.title: The Beard Tax
look.text: Imagine a Russian noble in 1700 standing before a clerk who holds up a small bronze token. To keep his beard, which his church has taught him is part of a man's God-given dignity, he must pay a yearly tax and carry the token as proof. Without it, an official may shave him on the spot. His grandfather would have called a beardless man half a woman. His son will grow up thinking beards are for peasants.
look.prompt: Why would a ruler spend political capital on something as small as beards? What was Peter really trying to change?

check.q: Why did Peter travel to Western Europe in 1697?
choices: To learn how Europeans built ships, made weapons and ran states
check.why: Peter worked in shipyards and visited workshops and governments to bring their skills back to Russia.

check.q: What did the Table of Ranks change?
choices: It made noble status depend on service rather than birth
It moved the capital to St. Petersburg
check.why: Under the 1722 system, rank came from serving in the army or government, and commoners could rise into the nobility.

check.q: Which statement about Peter's reforms is best supported?
choices: They made Russia a European power while hardening absolutism and serfdom
check.why: Peter's navy, army and capital made Russia a great power, but he paid for them with heavier taxes, harsher serfdom and more centralized rule.

lessons.title: Louis XIV and the Absolute State
lessons.mainIdea: Louis XIV of France claimed that all authority came from God through the king, and built Versailles, a professional bureaucracy and a huge army to make that claim real.
reading: Louis XIV became king of France in 1643, at four years old, and reigned for seventy-two years. As a boy he lived through a revolt of nobles that drove the royal family out of Paris. He never forgot it. When he took personal control of the government in 1661, he set out to make sure no noble, no parliament and no church could ever challenge the king again. The idea behind this was *absolutism*: the belief that a monarch holds complete power, answerable only to God.

Louis's tools were money, officials and spectacle. His finance minister, Colbert, built up French industry, taxed trade and tried to keep gold inside the kingdom, a policy called *mercantilism*. Royal agents called intendants ran the provinces, bypassing local nobles. And Louis built *Versailles*, a palace outside Paris so vast that thousands of nobles lived there at his expense. Competing for the honor of handing the king his shirt in the morning, they had no time to plot rebellion. Louis called himself the Sun King: everything revolved around him.

Absolutism demanded one faith. In 1685 Louis revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had protected French Protestants for nearly a century. Hundreds of thousands of them, often skilled craftsmen and merchants, fled to England, the Netherlands, Prussia and America, taking their skills with them. Louis also spent most of his reign at war, expanding France's borders and bankrupting its treasury. By his death in 1715 his army was the largest in Europe and his people were exhausted by taxes and famine.

Was absolutism as absolute as it claimed? Historians point out that Louis still had to bargain with provincial assemblies, sell government offices to raise cash, and tolerate tax exemptions for nobles and clergy. The king could not simply command; he had to persuade, reward and buy. But the model he set, of a ruler standing above all rivals and embodying the state, was copied by kings across Europe and challenged, within a century, by revolution.

words.d: the belief that a monarch holds complete power over the state, answerable only to God
the policy of building national wealth by exporting more than you import and keeping gold and silver in the kingdom
Louis XIV's enormous palace outside Paris, where he kept the nobility under his eye

look.title: A Bishop Explains Royal Power
look.text: Bishop Bossuet, who tutored Louis XIV's son, wrote that royal authority is sacred, because God establishes kings as his ministers and rules peoples through them. He argued that the king's power is absolute, that no one may judge the king but God, and that a subject who attacks the king attacks God himself.
look.cite: Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, Politics Drawn from the Words of Holy Scripture, France, written in the 1670s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: If a king's power comes only from God, who can hold him accountable? What would a subject who disagreed with this argument need to claim instead?

check.q: What childhood experience shaped Louis XIV's approach to ruling?
choices: A revolt of nobles that drove the royal family from Paris
A plague that killed his tutors
A war with Spain he witnessed
check.why: The noble revolt of his boyhood convinced Louis that the king must never again be at the mercy of powerful subjects.

check.q: How did Versailles help Louis control the nobility?
choices: Nobles living there competed for royal favor instead of plotting at home
It was a prison for rebellious lords
It was so far away that nobles could not reach it
check.why: Thousands of nobles lived at the palace, absorbed in ceremony and rivalry for the king's attention, under his constant eye.

check.q: What was one result of revoking the Edict of Nantes in 1685?
choices: Hundreds of thousands of skilled Protestants left France
check.why: French Protestants fled to rival countries, taking crafts, trade skills and money with them.

lessons.title: England's Constitutional Road
lessons.mainIdea: England fought a civil war, executed one king and expelled another, and by 1689 had settled that Parliament, not the crown alone, held the power to tax, legislate and limit the monarch.
reading: England's kings wanted what Louis had, and could not get it. Charles I, who came to the throne in 1625, tried to rule without *Parliament*, the assembly of nobles and elected gentry that by custom had to approve new taxes. He collected money by other means and ruled alone for eleven years. When he finally needed Parliament to pay for a war in 1640, its members demanded limits on his power instead. In 1642 the quarrel became a civil war between the king's supporters and Parliament's army.

Parliament won. In January 1649 Charles was tried for treason against his own people and beheaded in front of his palace. It was the first time a European monarch had been executed by a court in his subjects' name. The general Oliver Cromwell ruled a republic for a decade, but it depended on the army and on him. When he died in 1658 no one could hold it together, and in 1660 Parliament invited Charles's son back as Charles II. The question of who held final power was still open.

It was settled in 1688. James II, a Catholic, tried to override Parliament's laws and appoint Catholics to office. When his wife bore a son who would be raised Catholic, leading nobles invited James's Protestant daughter Mary and her Dutch husband William to invade. James fled without a battle. Because almost no blood was shed, the English called it the *Glorious Revolution*. William and Mary took the throne in 1689 on terms Parliament set.

Those terms were written into the English *Bill of Rights* of 1689. The monarch could not suspend laws, raise taxes or keep a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. Elections had to be free and parliamentary debate could not be punished. Subjects could petition the king, and cruel and unusual punishments were banned. It was not democracy; only a small fraction of men could vote. But it established that the ruler was under the law, and it gave English colonists in America a set of rights they would one day insist on.

lessons.title: Paying for Power
lessons.mainIdea: Every early modern state faced the same problem, paying for bigger armies, and the ones that could borrow cheaply and tax reliably won the wars.
reading: Armies grew enormously between 1500 and 1750. A large European army in 1500 might number thirty thousand men. By 1700 France alone kept several hundred thousand under arms. Muskets, cannon, uniforms, fortresses and warships all cost money, and soldiers had to be paid or they mutinied. Historians call this the military revolution, and it forced rulers everywhere to become tax collectors on a scale the world had never seen.

States found money in different ways. The Ottomans and Mughals taxed land directly and paid many officials with the income of assigned districts. France used *tax farming*: it sold the right to collect a tax to private financiers, who paid the crown up front and then squeezed the taxpayers for a profit. Spain lived on American silver until it ran short, then borrowed from foreign bankers and defaulted repeatedly. Nobles and clergy in France and Spain were largely exempt, so the burden fell on peasants and townspeople.

The winners were the states that could borrow. In 1694 England created the *Bank of England* to lend to the government, and Parliament guaranteed the interest with specific taxes. Because lenders trusted that Parliament would pay, England could borrow huge sums at low rates. This *national debt* let a small country fight France for decades. The Dutch Republic had done the same earlier. A king who could not be trusted to repay, like Louis XIV or the kings of Spain, paid far more to borrow far less.

Money also shaped rights. Rulers who needed taxes had to bargain with those who paid them. Where assemblies like Parliament controlled the purse, they could trade money for limits on royal power. Where kings could tax without asking, as in France and Russia, assemblies withered. The connection between taxation and representation was not an American invention; it was the central struggle of the age, and the Americans inherited it.

lessons.title: The Enlightenment
lessons.mainIdea: Thinkers of the 1700s argued that reason could discover laws of government as science had discovered laws of nature, and that legitimate power rests on the consent of the governed.
reading: If Newton could find the laws that governed the planets, could reason find the laws that should govern people? Thinkers across Europe in the 1700s believed it could. Historians call their movement the *Enlightenment*. Its center was France, its language was the printed pamphlet and the coffeehouse debate, and its targets were absolute monarchy, religious persecution and any claim that people should obey simply because they always had.

The English philosopher John Locke laid the foundation. Writing in 1690, just after the Glorious Revolution, he argued that all people are born with *natural rights* to life, liberty and property, and that governments exist to protect those rights. Rulers govern only with the *consent of the governed*. If a government attacks the rights it was created to protect, the people may replace it. Every phrase of that argument would reappear in the American Declaration of Independence in 1776.

French thinkers pushed further. Montesquieu, in 1748, studied governments from China to England and concluded that liberty survives only when power is divided: those who make laws, those who enforce them and those who judge should be separate branches that check each other. Voltaire attacked religious intolerance with wit and made a career of defending its victims. Rousseau argued in 1762 that a just government expresses the will of the people as a whole. Diderot's Encyclopedia gathered the era's knowledge into volumes that the French crown tried and failed to suppress.

The Enlightenment had blind spots and critics. Most of its thinkers were men who did not extend rights to women, and several defended slavery or wrote of non-Europeans with contempt; others, like the marquis de Condorcet, argued that rights had to include everyone. Some monarchs, like Frederick of Prussia and Catherine of Russia, admired the philosophers while keeping absolute power. Yet the ideas escaped their authors. Within a generation they would be used by revolutionaries in Philadelphia, Paris and Haiti.

lessons.title: Comparing the Empires
lessons.mainIdea: Empires of this era differed in how they treated religious minorities, how open they were to trade, and what they built, and those choices shaped their strength.
reading: Put the empires side by side and patterns appear. On religion, the Ottomans let Christians and Jews run their own communities. Akbar's Mughals abolished the tax on non-Muslims and welcomed every faith at court, until Aurangzeb reversed it. Louis XIV expelled his Protestants. Tokugawa Japan executed Christians. Tolerance was not a matter of East or West; it was a choice each state made, usually because of who it needed and what it feared.

Trade shows a similar spread. The Mughals and Ottomans welcomed foreign merchants because they profited from them; Indian cotton and Persian silk flowed out, and silver flowed in. Louis's France and the English tried to control trade for the state's benefit through mercantilist rules. The Qing allowed European trade but confined it to Canton. Japan shut the door to a crack. The more a state depended on customs duties and merchants, the more open it tended to be.

Every one of these rulers built to impress. Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal, Shah Abbas's Isfahan, the Ottoman mosques of Istanbul, Louis's Versailles, Peter's St. Petersburg and the Qing palaces of Beijing were all statements in stone: this state is rich, ordered and eternal. Art followed power. Mughal painters recorded court life in miniatures; Ottoman calligraphers and tile makers decorated mosques; French playwrights and composers performed for the Sun King. Japan's peace produced popular art for city dwellers instead: woodblock prints and kabuki theater.

Which choices made a state strong? Tolerance of useful minorities usually paid off, as the flight of French Protestants showed. Openness to trade brought silver and knowledge but also foreign pressure, as China and India would learn after 1750. Reliable taxes and honest borrowing mattered more than palaces. And a state that rested on one extraordinary ruler, as Safavid Persia and Mughal India did, was only as strong as the next ruler turned out to be.

lessons.title: Why Empires Faded
lessons.mainIdea: By 1750 the Safavids had fallen, the Mughals had fragmented and the Ottomans had stalled, undone by costly wars, succession fights, money troubles and rising rivals.
reading: In 1683 an Ottoman army besieged Vienna for the second time and was routed by a relief force led by the king of Poland. Over the next decades the Ottomans lost Hungary and their aura of invincibility. In 1722 Afghan rebels captured Isfahan and ended the Safavid dynasty. After Aurangzeb died in 1707, Mughal power drained away to regional governors and Maratha armies; in 1739 a Persian invader sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne. Three empires that had dominated the world in 1600 were shadows by 1750.

The causes overlapped. War was the first. Aurangzeb spent twenty-five years campaigning in the south and gained little but debt and enemies. The Ottomans fought Persia, Austria, Russia and Venice, often at once. Second was succession. None of these empires had a clear rule for who came next, so the death of a ruler often meant a war among his sons, and the winner inherited a divided state. Third was money. Tax income fell as provincial officials kept more for themselves, while European silver, once a blessing, drove inflation that ate soldiers' pay.

Fourth, and hardest to see at the time, was the growing strength of rivals. European states, forced to compete with each other in a crowded continent, had built better cannon, disciplined infantry, navies and, above all, reliable credit. Their trading companies were armed corporations with their own soldiers. When Mughal power collapsed in Bengal, the English East India Company was there to fill it. In 1757 its small army defeated the region's ruler at Plassey and began to govern Indian provinces directly.

Historians warn against reading the story backward. In 1750 China was still the world's largest economy, the Ottomans still ruled a vast territory, and no one in Delhi or Istanbul imagined that a trading company from a small island would rule India. Decline was not destiny. But the pattern is worth studying, because it repeats: states that stop adapting their armies, their finances and their institutions are overtaken by those that keep changing, whatever their size.
